answer: A CDN sits transparently between the user and the origin. The origin is a generic term for wherever the content lives: an S3 bucket, a backend server, literally anything you want served through the CDN. The user only talks to the CDN; only the CDN calls the origin, on a miss.
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'A CDN transparently sits between your user and your origin.' 'Origin is a generic term for wherever the content lives: an S3 bucket, a backend server, literally anything you want served through your CDN.'

answer: A CDN is not something you push things to. It pulls: it sits transparently between user and origin, serves cached bytes if it has them, otherwise fetches the same path from the origin, caches and serves it. Most CDNs offer APIs nowadays, but that is not their main job.
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'A CDN is not something you push things to. Most CDNs offer APIs nowadays, but that is not their main job. Their job is to sit transparently between the user and the origin.' 'Nothing is pushed to it: it pulls.'

answer: The backend's bandwidth is spent on something almost static (images hardly ever change), and images are huge (1-10 MB) - spending 10 MB of an API server's bandwidth on one is 'a crime'; the bytes go through the same network card every API call uses, and you want API servers lean and fast. Distance makes it worse: a server in Singapore sending 10 MB to a US user slows everything down.
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'The backend server's bandwidth is being spent on something almost static... images are huge: 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 MB. Spending 10 MB of an API server's bandwidth to serve one of them is “a crime”. You want your API servers lean and fast. Distance makes it worse...'

answer: Just one origin URL: a mapping called a CDN property (CloudFront calls it a distribution) from your subdomain on the provider, e.g. a.mycdn.net, to an origin, e.g. arpitbhayani.me. Any request to a.mycdn.net is forwarded to arpitbhayani.me. You never configure individual URLs.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'All it asks for is one origin URL... That configuration is a mapping, called a CDN property: your subdomain on the provider, say a.mycdn.net, mapped to an origin, arpitbhayani.me.'

answer: The browser does an ordinary DNS resolution of the hostname in the URL and sends the request to that IP; resolving a.mycdn.net returns the CDN provider's IP (classic DNS config on Route 53 or your domain provider like GoDaddy/Namecheap; for your own hostname, a CNAME to the CDN's edge hostname). The browser doesn't know it is a CDN.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'The browser doesn't know whether a host is a CDN... it does a DNS resolution of whatever hostname is in the URL and sends the request to that IP address. Resolving a.mycdn.net returns the CDN provider's IP address. That is classic DNS configuration, done on Route 53 or at your domain provider...'

answer: 1) Browser asks DNS for a.mycdn.net and gets the CDN provider's IP. 2) It sends GET /system-design/logo.png to the CDN, which looks up the origin configured for property a.mycdn.net: arpitbhayani.me. 3) It checks its cache: nothing (first request). It swaps the host, keeps the path: arpitbhayani.me/system-design/logo.png. 4) The CDN itself requests that URL from the origin, which answers as it always does. 5) The CDN caches the bytes and returns them to the user.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2 Fig 2·c steps and §2.3: 'the CDN first checks: do I have anything cached for this path? No... So the CDN itself makes the request to arpitbhayani.me/system-design/logo.png. The origin generates the response... sends it to the CDN, which caches it and sends it to the user.'

answer: The host changes (the CDN discards its own hostname and puts the configured origin in its place); the path stays the same.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'It swaps the host and keeps the path: a.mycdn.net/system-design/logo.png becomes arpitbhayani.me/system-design/logo.png.'

answer: It goes to the CDN as always; the CDN already has the image cached and serves it directly (a hit) - the request never enters your backend. The origin is hit again only when the cached copy expires (TTL) or is invalidated.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'The next request for the same path goes to the CDN, just like always. This time the CDN already has the image cached and serves it directly.' Clip 2·1: 'Every later request is a hit... When the copy expires, one request refills it.'

answer: No. The CDN caches whatever it gets as a set of bytes: API/JSON responses, text files, images, videos, fragments, HTML pages. Caveat from the page: it only caches responses that are cacheable per origin headers/CDN policy; e.g. Cloudflare doesn't cache HTML or JSON by default.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'Whatever it gets back, it caches as a set of bytes... API responses, JSON responses, text files, images, videos, fragments: all of them can be cached on a CDN. What a CDN won't do is cache everything automatically.' 'the common belief that only images can be cached on a CDN is wrong.'

answer: On a hit the request doesn't enter your backend, saving backend bandwidth and cutting infrastructure cost: you need a couple of servers instead of hundreds, since only a few requests (one per cache invalidation) reach the backend. Rule of thumb: you keep infra cost down while paying almost the same to the CDN, and get extra performance; actual savings depend on traffic and hit ratio.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'That saves your backend servers' bandwidth and cuts the cost of the infrastructure. You need a couple of servers instead of hundreds...' 'you keep your infrastructure cost down while paying almost the same amount to the CDN, and get extra performance on top'.

answer: No - it's a myth; pseudo privacy. Photos are on the CDN and anyone holding a valid URL can open them until it expires (short-term access, e.g. a follower copies the URL). It makes barging in difficult, not impossible.

answer: On the owner's own private profile (confirmed private), inspect a photo, copy its image URL (fbcdn.net with oh/oe params), paste it in an incognito window - the image opens. 'Privacy is a myth, my friend.'

answer: CDN domain (fbcdn.net, e.g. instagram.fblr22-1.fna.fbcdn.net), CDN path (/ul/), image name containing the random ID, then query parameters: ig_cache_key (Instagram cache key), oh (hash/signature), oe (most probably expiry), nc_sid etc. (CDN's own). The query parameters make photos 'private' - more exactly they make the URL expire and tamper-proof; real privacy is the API server deciding who gets the URL.

answer: It has no authentication of its own and is 100% stateless (doesn't know users/follows). It relies on timed signatures, like JWT: expiry baked into the URL with a signature over it; the CDN validates the signature and checks expiry.

answer: A truly private platform can't use a CDN: every request (upload and download) goes through your API server, which checks per request whether the user may read that image. answer: An expiration time baked into the URL's metadata, with a signature attached over it so no one can change that time; the CDN validates the signature and checks expiry. They work exactly like a JWT (signature sometimes called a 'certificate').

answer: URL is rendered through an IMG tag; request goes to the CDN; CDN extracts query params (oe, oh); checks signature valid and not expired; returns image if both hold, else bad-URL error. evidence: Ch5 §5.2: 'The URL is rendered through an IMG tag; the request goes to the CDN; the CDN extracts the query parameters, checks that the signature is valid and that the URL hasn't expired, and returns the image if both hold, otherwise a bad-URL error.' §5.1: 'The board put it as “the URL is short lived because certs are short lived”.'
